rejected.title: The Estates-General of 1789
card: The Estates-General was an assembly of representatives of the three estates: clergy, nobles and the Third Estate. Louis XVI agreed to call it to deal with the financial crisis. It met at Versailles in May 1789.
The Third Estate sent about as many deputies as the other two estates combined. Many of these deputies were lawyers and other educated men.

The assembly deadlocked over how to vote. The clergy and nobles wanted one vote per estate, so they could outvote the Third Estate two to one. The Third Estate wanted one vote per deputy, with the three estates meeting together.

After weeks of stalemate, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly in June 1789. It claimed to speak for the whole French people, and it acted without waiting for the approval of the other estates.
rejected.remember: A fight over how to vote led the Third Estate to claim the right to speak for the people as the National Assembly.

a.q: Why did the voting method matter so much to the Third Estate?
opts: Voting by estate let the clergy and nobles outvote it
Voting by deputy let the nobles outvote it
Voting by estate gave the king the deciding vote
Voting by deputy removed its right to send deputies
a.why: If each estate had one vote, the clergy and nobles could combine to outvote the Third Estate two to one, even though it had about as many deputies as both of them together. Voting by deputy would have given each of its many deputies a vote of equal weight, which is why it wanted that method.
a.clue: Count the votes if each estate gets only one.

b.q: In June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. What was the main meaning of this step?
opts: It claimed authority to act without the other two estates
It gave in to the demand for one vote for each estate
It handed the deadlock to the king to settle for it
It agreed to wait for the clergy and nobles to join it
b.why: By renaming itself, the Third Estate claimed to speak for the whole French people and to act without the approval of the other estates. It did not accept voting by estate, which had caused the deadlock, and it did not ask the king to settle the matter.
b.clue: Ask who the deputies were still waiting for, if anyone.

flags: Question b, wording: The right option is the only one that uses the word 'nation', which echoes the stem ('National Assembly') and the clue. The distractors (going home, being dissolved) are implausible, so a student can pick the answer without knowing the idea.

Why (a) says the clergy and nobles could 'always beat' the Third Estate, but the card says only that they 'could outvote' it. 'Always' overstates the card.
Why (a) refers to the Third Estate's 'larger number of deputies'. The card says it had about as many deputies as the other two estates combined, not more, so the explanation contradicts the card.

version.title: The Estates-General of 1789
card: The Estates-General was an assembly of deputies from the three estates: clergy, nobles and the Third Estate. It had not met since 1614.
Louis XVI called it to solve the crisis, and it opened at Versailles in May 1789. The Third Estate had about as many deputies as the other two estates combined.

It deadlocked over voting. One vote per estate let the clergy and nobles outvote the Third Estate two to one, while one vote per deputy, in a joint meeting, would give the Third Estate half the votes.
In June 1789, after weeks of stalemate, the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. It claimed to speak for the whole nation and acted without waiting for the other estates or the king.
version.remember: A deadlock over voting led the Third Estate to claim power for the nation as the National Assembly.

a.q: Why did the Third Estate want one vote per deputy, not one vote per estate?
opts: It would hold half the votes instead of one in three
It had fewer deputies than the other two estates combined
It wanted each estate to meet and vote on its own
It would let the king break deadlocks between estates
a.why: With one vote per estate, the Third Estate held one vote in three, so the clergy and nobles could outvote it. Its deputies matched the other two estates combined, so one vote per deputy would give it half the votes. It did not have fewer deputies, which is why the method mattered so much.
a.clue: Count its share of the votes each way.

b.q: On 17 June 1789 the Third Estate declared itself the National Assembly. Why do historians see this as a revolutionary step?
opts: It claimed to speak for the nation, not just one estate
It accepted that each estate would vote on its own
It handed the voting dispute back to the king to settle
It let the clergy and nobles block whatever it decided
b.why: The deputies claimed authority from the whole nation and acted without the other estates or the king, which broke with the old order. They did not accept voting by estate, and they did not hand the dispute back to the king to settle.
b.clue: Whose approval did it stop waiting for?

a.best: It would hold half the votes instead of one in three

b.best: It claimed to speak for the nation, not just one estate
